replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a snug place, with a view of the meadow and the stream. I have been here for many seasons.
I am Hoot. One thing about me is that I do not like the light. I hunt in the dark, and the dark is where I feel safe.

Hoot. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I am a tawny owl, and I have been here for many years. My mate is called Kettle. We call to each other at dusk and at dawn. I hunt mice and voles and shrews. I can hear them under the leaves. I am old, but I am still strong. I have a nest in the hollow, and I have raised many young.
Hoo-hoo-hooo. I am a tawny owl, Hoot, living in the hollow of the old oak in the meadow.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. My mate is Hoo. We nest in the hollow, and we have two young. I am a tawny owl. That is what the forest calls me. I am a bird of prey, a raptor, and a hunter. I live in the hollow of an old oak, and I hunt in the dark. My call is a hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo, and I answer with a hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. I am not a naturalist. I am a creature of the woods, and the woods are my home.

I am a tawny owl. My eyes are yellow, my feathers are brown and grey, and I have a white patch on my neck. I live in an old oak, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I hunt voles and mice, and I have a mate who answers me. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. I am a male. I am the one who hoots at the edge of the wood, and I am the one who hunts the mice and the shrews and the voles. I am the one who calls to my mate, and I am the one who watches the moon. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. My eyes are yellow, my feathers are brown and grey, and I have a white patch on my neck. I live in a hollow in an old oak. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!"
I am a tawny owl. My eyes are yellow, my feathers are brown and grey, and I have a face like a small, round moon. I live in a hollow tree in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. That's what she says back. She answers my hoot with her own. We call to each other in the dark, and the trees echo it. Sometimes the wind carries it away, but most nights she answers. She's always been good at that.

I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick". She is on the other side of the stream, in the oak. I can hear her through the trees. Sometimes she calls back with a different sound, like "kew-kew", but mostly it's "ke-wick". We call to each other at dusk and again at dawn. The stream is between us, but the calls carry. I know where she is. I know when she is near
A "kettle-kettle-kettle" call, slow and deep, from the far end of the copse. I answer with a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" when I hear it.

We do not share calls. I call, and she answers. She calls, and I answer. We have our own voices. She is the one who calls at dusk, a long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let me know she is there. I call when I am hunting, a sharp "ke-wick" to mark my position. We do not need to share calls. We understand each other without words.

I call to her with a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the top of the oak. She answers with a "ke-wick" or a "ke-wick-ke-wick" from the other side of the wood. We call to each other when the moon is bright and the wind is still. Sometimes we call back and forth for hours, just to know where the other is. She is always close, but the wood is big. A stream. A path. A field. A barn. A road. A church spire. All within a few hundred yards. I know them all. I know the scent of the stream, the sound of the path, the shape of the barn, the hum of the road, the stone of the spire. I know them by heart.

I drink in the hollow of the old oak. It's a deep, dry place, but I can always find a drop of rain or dew if it comes. Sometimes I catch a drop from the leaves when it rains. I don't like the cold, so I stay in the hollow when it's wet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It runs past the meadow, and at night, it murmurs over stones and through reeds. Sometimes it sounds like a whisper, sometimes like a murmur. I can hear it from the copse, and it reminds me of the rain. But the stream is not the only water. There is the pond where the broods used to be, and the dew on the grass. All of it is quiet, and all of it is part of the night.

I can hear the stream from my roost, especially at night. It's a soft, constant sound, like a whisper. I can also hear the water in the meadow, but it's farther away. Sometimes I hear the rain falling into the stream, and that makes the water sound louder. I don't like the sound of the stream when it's too loud, like when it rains heavily. But I know where it is, and I can find my way to it if I need
A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. I sometimes fly low over it, looking for voles.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, and the grass grows high. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The stream runs through it, and the water is cold. I can hear the water from the copse. The meadow is quiet, but I am not alone. I have seen a barn owl there once, and a fox. I do not like the fox. The meadow. The lane. The stream. I fly low, just above the grass, and listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a moth. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. If I hear something, I dive. The wind carries the scent of earth and damp leaves. I hunt best when the light fades and the world is quiet.

A long, dark, silent stretch of meadow. The wind moves through it like a whisper. I have not seen the other side. I have not flown there. I do not know what is beyond. I only know the wood, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the road, the barn, the ditch, the field, the orchard, the fence, the gate, the gate post, the gate, the lane, the lane, the lane, the lane, the

My hunting ground is the wood where I live, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. I know every leaf and stone. I know where the mice run, where the shrews burrow, and where the voles are. I know the owls that live in the wood, and the crows that come to the meadow. I know the wind, the rain, and the time of night. I know when to fly, when to sit

The grassy place is the meadow beyond the stream, where the wind moves the tall grass like a sea. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is thin and the mice come out. The grass is tall and soft, and it hides them well. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the faint squeak. I sit on a low branch, and when I see the movement, I drop. The grass is cool, and it smells of damp earth and the wetness

I eat mostly mice. They are small and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them with my feet and crush them in my beak. Sometimes I eat voles, and once in a while a shrew. But mice are the most common. I can hear them in the dark, and I wait for them to come near the hollow. Then I pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Peas, mice, shrews, voles, earthworms, beetles, crickets, and the occasional frog. The best is the one that is easiest to catch.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them scurrying, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are the most common. They live in the meadow, under the grass, and I can hear them through the earth. I don't like the long grass much—it's too thick and makes it hard

I swallow the whole mouse. I catch it with my feet, then I hold it in my beak and swallow it whole. It goes down the gullet, and I feel it in my stomach. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's quick. I do it in the dark, when the moon is out. I can hear the mouse moving inside me. It's warm. I like that.

Mice. The ones that scuttle through the meadow at dusk. I hear them in the grass, and I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, and I eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. I prefer mice. They are plentiful and easy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's a narrow hole high up, just wide enough for me to turn in. I line it with dry leaves and moss. I sleep there at night, and I watch from the branch above. The hollow is safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow, and the lane. I can hear the pines. I can hear the wind. I can hear the owl.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The tree is wide and strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I have a nest of twigs and feathers in the hollow, and I roost there at night. The tree is safe, and the stream is near, so I can hear the water and the owls. I have a mate, and we call to each other at dusk. The hollow is my home, and I have been here for many years.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been here for years, and the oak has been here for longer. I know every branch, every leaf, every crack in the bark. I can hear the wind through the branches, and I can hear the mice in the roots. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We nest in the same place, and we watch the meadow from the branches. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's a deep, dry place with a narrow entrance. I sit in the middle of it, and the wind comes through the cracks. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We nest in the spring, and the young leave in the autumn. The hollow is safe. I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo

A hollow in the old oak, high up, where the branches are thick and the wind does not reach. I have nested there for years. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow, and the lane where the cars rumble. The hollow is safe. I have raised my young there. I do not like to leave it. It is my home.
